sections.h2: Who sends and who values a Franklin County property tax bill?
sections.html:
Franklin County splits the job between the Tax Commissioner, who bills and collects, and the Board of Tax Assessors, who set values and approve exemptions. The Tax Commissioner does not set value or millage rates. The county commissioners and the county school board set those rates each year, and the money supports the county, the schools, the Industrial Building Authority and the State of Georgia.

The Tax Commissioner's office is at 1221 Hull Avenue in Carnesville, the county seat, with a mailing address of PO Box 100, Carnesville, GA 30521. Call 706-384-3455 between 8:00 a.m. and 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday. Questions about values, exemptions and returns go to the Tax Assessor at 706-384-4896.

sections.h2: How is a Franklin County tax bill figured?
sections.html:
Assessed value is 40 percent of fair market value. The office subtracts any exemption to reach a net assessed value, then multiplies by the millage rate, where one mill is $1 per $1,000 of assessed value. Fair market value is defined as what a knowledgeable buyer would pay and a willing seller would accept in an arm's-length sale.

Owners who have changed or acquired property file a real estate return (form PT-50r) with the assessor between January 1 and April 1. Skipping a required return carries a 10 percent penalty on the value not returned, plus interest. If nothing has changed since the prior year, the return is optional.

sections.h2: What are the main Franklin County property tax rules at a glance?
sections.html:
The table gathers the figures a seller most often needs. Each row comes from the Franklin County Tax Office or the county's government site.

Franklin County property tax basics (Franklin County Tax Office and Franklin County government pages)
ItemWhat the county says
Bills dueNormally November 15
Interest after the due date1 percent per month
Added penalty10 percent if unpaid within 90 days of the deadline
Assessment appeal window45 days from the notice date
Homestead and return filingJanuary 1 to April 1
Mobile home return and permitOn or before May 1
Tax salesFirst Tuesday of a month, in front of the courthouse

The 10 percent penalty is not applied to homesteaded property whose tax liability is under $500.

sections.h2: What happens if I pay Franklin County property tax late?
sections.html:
Interest starts the day after the deadline, and the added penalty follows at 90 days. A tax lien (also called a fifa or execution) is then recorded with the Clerk of Superior Court. These records are public, and the tax office warns that credit bureaus may use them and that it has no control over how.

A lien is released only when the delinquent taxes are paid in full. If they stay unpaid the tax commissioner, who serves as ex-officio sheriff, can levy the property and auction it. The office calls that a last resort, preferring other collection methods first.

Anyone selling with an unpaid bill should call 706-384-3455 and ask what is owed through the closing date, including interest and any recorded lien.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Franklin County assessment?
sections.html:
File within 45 days of the date on the assessment notice. The appeal goes to the Board of Tax Assessors first, which reviews it and tells you its decision. If nothing changes, the appeal is forwarded to the county Board of Equalization, which holds a hearing, and you can go on to Superior Court afterward by sending written notice to the assessors.

Arbitration is offered in place of the Board of Equalization. Grounds are limited to taxability, value and uniformity compared with similar properties. The county says a complaint about the amount of tax levied is not a valid ground, because the millage rate is set by other bodies.

sections.h2: Which Franklin County exemptions and relief programs exist?
sections.html:
You apply once with the Tax Assessor, and the exemption renews itself unless ownership changes or you want a different type. You must own and occupy the home on January 1. The county's exemptions page and the tax office FAQ both give April 1 as the last filing day, although an older page on the tax office site still says March 1, so file early and ask the assessor to confirm.

  • Standard homestead: $2,000 off the 40 percent assessed value for state, county and school taxes, as the county page prints it.
  • Age 65 and older, local exemption: $20,000 against all taxes on the homestead.
  • Age 62 and older, floating exemption: tied to natural increases in value, with an income cap of $30,000.
  • Disabled veterans: $100,896, extended to an unremarried surviving spouse or minor children.
  • Tax deferral: owners 62 or older with gross income of $15,000 or less may defer payment, generally until ownership changes or the deferred amount plus interest reaches 85 percent of fair market value.

The board of tax assessors makes the final eligibility call, and a denied applicant must be notified and may appeal.

sections.h2: How are farm and timber land taxed in Franklin County?
sections.html:
Franklin County is rural, so land programs matter. Qualifying agricultural property can be assessed at 30 percent instead of 40 percent. Under conservation use, farm and timber land is valued at its current use rather than market value, but the owner signs a covenant to keep it in that use for ten years. Applications are due by April 1 with a $25 recording fee.

Breaking the covenant brings a penalty of twice the taxes saved, with some exceptions: no penalty on death or condemnation, and a lighter one for illness or foreclosure. If the land is sold and the buyer keeps using it as covenanted, no penalty applies, but the buyer must sign the covenant.

Standing timber is not taxed until it is sold or harvested, and then on 100 percent of its fair market value. Mobile and modular homes are personal property taxed each year, and a location permit requires that year's tax to be paid in full.

sections.h2: What is the tax sale and redemption process in Franklin County?
sections.html:
Sales are scheduled for the first Tuesday of a month in front of the courthouse, advertised weekly for four weeks in the Franklin County Citizen. Bidding opens at the total of taxes, fees and interest on the parcel.

The owner, a creditor or anyone with an interest can redeem during the twelve months after the sale. Redemption means paying the buyer the sale amount, taxes the buyer paid afterward, special assessments, and a premium of 20 percent for the first year or part of a year and 10 percent for each added year or part. The buyer cannot take possession, collect rent or improve the property during that period. The county tells readers to take foreclosure questions to an attorney.

sections.h2: What does the Census Bureau say about Franklin County?
sections.html:
QuickFacts estimates 25,948 residents in July 2025, up 10.8 percent from the 2020 base, across 261.35 square miles of land at about 90 people per square mile. The county has 11,475 housing units and a 77.2 percent owner-occupied rate. The 2020 to 2024 median value of an owner-occupied home is $179,000, median household income is $53,046, and 19.6 percent of residents are 65 or older.

That older share and the lower value mean exemptions for seniors carry real weight here, and many households will have no mortgage: median monthly owner costs without one are $432, against $1,432 with one.

faqs.q: When are Franklin County, Georgia property taxes due?
faqs.a: Normally November 15. After that, 1 percent interest is added each month, and a 10 percent penalty applies to taxes still unpaid 90 days past the deadline.

faqs.q: Who do I call about my Franklin County property value?
faqs.a: The Franklin County Tax Assessor at 706-384-4896. The Tax Commissioner at 706-384-3455 handles billing and payment, not value.

faqs.q: How long can I appeal a Franklin County assessment?
faqs.a: 45 days from the date of the assessment notice. Appeals go to the Board of Tax Assessors, then the Board of Equalization or arbitration, then Superior Court.

faqs.q: Is there a senior exemption in Franklin County?
faqs.a: Yes. The county lists a local exemption of $20,000 for owners 65 and older, plus state exemptions for ages 62 and 65 with income limits and a deferral program for owners 62 or older with gross income of $15,000 or less.

faqs.q: What happens to a property sold at a Franklin County tax sale?
faqs.a: The owner, a creditor or another interested person can redeem it for twelve months by paying what the county page lists, including a 20 percent premium for the first year. The buyer cannot take possession during that time.
